source: iadopt-lab answer_form_check.py, arm named-first (the conventions test's plain prompt)
head:
Classify the scientific variable defined below with the I-ADOPT patterns.
Return one JSON object with these keys, in this order: "object_of_interest" (the entity whose property is measured, in a few words), "matrix_entity" (the entity that is the matrix, in a few words, or null when there is no matrix), "restrictions" (a list of the phrases of the definition that narrow the variable; [] when there are none), "property" (one property pattern number), "matrix" (one matrix pattern number, or null when there is no matrix), "context" (true or false: is a context object needed), "modifier" (true or false: is a statistical modifier involved) and "constraints" (a list of the constraint type names of the restrictions; [] when there are none). Return the JSON only.

PROPERTY PATTERNS
101 nominal: A nominal variable has values of equal importance that cannot be ranked in any particular order (non-ordinal), e.g., species of pests, colors. The values of these variables are usually indicated by words, ideally using controlled lists.
102 ordinal: An ordinal variable has values corresponding to a list of concepts that can be put in a certain order but are not measured. They are generally qualitative, and the classes can therefore only be ordered in relation to each other. Dates are also ordinal values.
103 boolean: A binary or boolean property allows exactly two values: true/false, good/bad. Quality flags are boolean.
104 count: Assigns to an entity a non-negative integer equal to the number of distinct related entities satisfying a declared relation and scope.
105 discrete: A unitless property with integer values (excluding counts) that are physically enforced. They can be constants or variable numbers.
106 length: Length of a discrete object. Length is a fundamental property. Examples are width, depth, height, circumference.
107 length ref: Length in relation to another object. Length is a fundamental property. Examples are width, depth, height, circumference.
108 distance: Length between two objects.
109 fundamental: Fundamental properties are physical quantities that are conventionally accepted as functionally independent of all others, excluding lengths. These are thermodynamic temperature, time, mass, amount of substance, luminous intensity, electric current.
110 fraction: A fraction is a ratio comparing a part to the whole where the quantities (quantitative property) are of the same kind.
111 property (cover): Cover expresses the fraction of a total reference area that is occupied by the Object of Interest.
112 geometric ratio: A unitless ratio comparing two geometric properties of the same kind to describe the intrinsic, static shape of a single object (e.g., Aspect Ratio).
113 dimensionless physical ratio: A quantity that describes physical relationships or the physical state of a system without an associated physical unit.
114 ratioless derived: A derived property without ratio-transformation from fundamental quantities like volume or area.
115 normalized: A relative quantity whose value is expressed relative to an explicit baseline, reference standard, or nominal state, rather than as an explicit physical ratio of two variable entities.
116 angle: An angle measured against a local/arbitrary reference frame (e.g., the angle between two intersecting pipes, or the joint angle of a knee).
117 direction: A spatial or angular measurement indicating the orientation, heading, or trajectory of an entity relative to a specified reference frame (vector).
118 event rate: A temporal property measuring the number of discrete, countable events or occurrences that take place within a specified period of time.
120 velocity: Vector property that measures the rate of change of an object's position with respect to time, combining both speed (magnitude) and direction.
121 massic number density: Count of individual entities per mass of a medium.
122 massic amount of substance: Mole per mass including molality (denominator is mass of the solvent component) and substance content (denominator is mass of the total mixture).
123 lineic density: Quantity per length, example is linear mass density.
124 normalized count: Count per entity.
125 volumic number density: Count per volume.
126 intrinsic: A property that is inherent to the substance's chemical composition and molecular structure, like plasticity, volumic density, absorbance.
127 areal density: Quantity per area.
128 concentration: Concentration describes how much of one substance (the solute) is present in another substance (the solvent) as a volume. Examples are mass and amount of substance concentration.
129 flux simplified: A ratio rate with an energy flow represented in a simplified way.
130 flux simple: A ratio rate with a material flow from a source to a target while the denominator is represented by an area.
131 flux complex: A ratio rate with a material flow from a source to a target. Complex representation is needed when there needs to be a constraint on the denominator.
132 index: An index acts as a proxy property that normalizes data against a specific base point or reference value to provide relative context rather than absolute measurement. While it sometimes aggregates multiple variables into a single score, its primary function is to make diverse data sets comparable over time or across different subjects.
133 distance ref: Length between two objects, where one of the two is constraint.
134 energy per mole: Energy per amount of substance (molar energy).
135 massic activity: Radioactivity content of chemical substance per mass.
136 statistical property: A statistical measure becomes a statistical property when it changes the dimension of the property of the measurement like variance and confidence interval.
137 instant: A time-instant value, e.g. 2026-08-15T13:29:14+02:00
138 interval: Properties resulting in quantitative numbers that represent ordered points along a continuous scale with equal, measurable distances between adjacent units, but without a true absolute zero point.
139 probability: Probability is a numerical measure of how likely a specific event is to occur. It quantifies chance or uncertainty on a scale strictly bounded between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%).
140 atomic derived property: A property that acts as an atomic (scalar) concept, derived from fundamental physical dimensions. Examples are acceleration and speed.
142 areic amount of substance: Amount of substance per area.

MATRIX PATTERNS
40 embedding material: The matrix must be of a different material than the object of interest. If the material is the same, the description component has a context object role.
41 natural container: A matrix is required when the object of interest is contained in a natural body.
42 artificial container: A matrix is required when the object of interest is contained in an artificial vessel.
43 natural process: A phenomenon in which the object is involved.
44 reference area: Is an area that acts as reference like a study area.
45 flow: Flow of material from one source to a target.

CONSTRAINT TYPES
A constraint is an explicit restriction in the definition that narrows the property, the object of interest, the matrix or the statistical modifier. The property, the object of interest and the matrix themselves are not constraints.
age: restricts the human subject or population to a defined age interval, specific age value, or life stage.
agent: an entity—either human, artificial, biological, or organizational—that senses its environment and acts upon it autonomously to achieve a specific goal or purpose.
cause: indicates the cause that explains why the constrained component occurs or holds
classification: systematic arrangement in groups or categories according to established criteria
composition: what the constrained component consists of: its constituents or the mixture it is
condition: a contextual circumstance or environmental feature that limits or qualifies the constrained component
criterion: A single principle, standard, or rule used to make a judgment or decision.
diameter: the length of a straight line through the center of an object or space
direction: specifies the spatial orientation, vector heading, or flow orientation (e.g., downward, northward, incoming, outward) of the observed phenomenon relative to a spatial coordinate system, physical boundary, or reference feature.
education: the systematic process of facilitating learning, acquiring knowledge, skills, values, beliefs, and habits through instruction, training, research, or discussion.
event: identifies a specific occurrence, process, or life-stage event (e.g., birth, flooding, surgical procedure) that bounds or triggers the observation, serving as a contextual anchor when explicit calendar time or duration is unknown or non-applicable.
location: provides a location-specific information about the constrained component
locomotion state: refers to the distinct physiological, kinematic, or mechanical mode of self-propelled movement exhibited by an organism
material type: provides a material type information about the constrained component
min temperature: a minimum temperature that the constrained component must reach for it to count
normalization: specifies the reference quantity to which a measurement is rescaled.
order: An order relation that formalizes the notion of sorting elements.
part: specifies a structural, anatomical, or biological sub-component (e.g., leaf, liver, root, surface layer) of an entity.
physical form: refers to the visible, structural, or material state of an object or substance, describing its physical appearance, state of matter, or spatial shape
process: refers to a process that occurs when measuring the property Or: a series of systematic, ordered actions or steps taken to achieve a specific end or result.
purity: specifies the degree of quality or purity of a substance or generally of the component
purpose: the purpose for which the constrained component is made, carried out or used
quantity: specifies the quantity in which the entity occurs
range: provides the range of allowed values
rating: an evaluation, assessment, or classification of something against a standardized scale or set of criteria.
reference: provides a reference point or information for the constrained component
region: specifies an area of land or space that shares unifying characteristics, setting it apart from surrounding areas
relationship: a significant connection, association, or involvement between two or more people, groups, or entities, characterized by mutual interaction, influence, or relevance.
reporting frequency: defines how often a final data point is reported
resistivity: an intrinsic physical property of a material that measures how strongly it opposes or resists the flow of electric current.
role: indicates the role a person might have in the context of the variable
sampling frequency: provides the sampling frequency that applies for the constrained component
source: specifies the source, provenance, or starting point of the constrained component
spatial distribution: defines the domain or criteria over which a statistical measure is calculated
spatial extent: indicates the spatial coverage within which the constrained component applies
state: indicates the physical, chemical or qualitative condition, including phases, of the constrained component
temporal extent: indicates the temporal coverage within which the constrained component applies
temporal reference: a linguistic mechanism, point of origin, or benchmark used to locate events, actions, or states in time relative to another point in time.
thickness: the thickness of the layer or film of the constrained component on which the variable is measured
threshold: defines the value limit that triggers a quality flag, indicating whether the measurement satisfies the threshold criterion.
time: provides time-specific information about the constrained component
vicinity: the surrounding area, neighborhood, or general proximity near a specific place or landmark.
volume: the volume of the sample or portion of the constrained component on which the value is measured
wavelength: the distance in the line of advance of a wave from any one point to the next point of corresponding phase
